strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across four benchmarks (InfographicVQA, ChartMuseum, ChartQAPro, HR-Bench 4K) with consistent improvements (3.6-11% gains)
Interesting recovery analysis showing 47-53% correction of minority-correct cases and 2.5-4.5% of zero-correct cases, demonstrating complementary reasoning paths
Practical training-free approach with cost-efficient inference (<$0.011 per sample for GPT-4o verdict)
Thorough ablation studies examining expert count, selection strategies, input modalities, and model pool compositions
Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of challenges in information-intensive VQA (precise localization and multi-hop reasoning)
Substantially outperforms tool-driven baseline DeepEyes by 12-21% despite not requiring training or explicit zoom-in operations
Extensive supplementary materials supporting reproducibility with detailed prompts, error analysis, and qualitative examples
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: straightforward application of established speculative decoding paradigm (Leviathan et al., 2023) to VQA with standard NLL-based consensus scoring primarily via prompt engineering

Incomplete cost accounting: reports only verdict inference cost in Table 5, not total pipeline cost including all k=5 draft model forward passes; no comparison of total SV cost vs. single GPT-4o run on original image

Expert selection mechanism lacks rigor: weak justification for relative NLL formulation, limited exploration of alternatives (only best-reference compared), no ablation isolating consensus selection contribution, cross-all strategy is simplistic

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: error decomposability claimed but not rigorously analyzed, why reasoning synthesis beats majority voting unclear beyond single example, zero-correct recovery mechanism unexplained and small in magnitude (2.5-4.5%)

Missing key baseline comparisons: learned ensemble aggregators (Qi et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025) cited but not evaluated, no comparison with other reasoning synthesis or ensemble aggregation methods

Verdict model dependency and hidden tuning: results strongly depend on verdict choice (GPT-4o underperforms Qwen72B on HR-Bench 4K: 71.4% vs 73.1%), Section 4.3 admits task-specific tuning required, undermines 'training-free' claims

Narrow evaluation scope: restricted to information-dense structured images (infographics, charts) with no evaluation on general VQA, scene understanding, or other vision tasks limiting generalizability

Prompt engineering dependency and unclear reproducibility: different datasets require different CoT templates, no sensitivity analysis to prompt variations, reproducibility across prompt strategies unclear
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; all improvements reported as point estimates without uncertainty quantification
Modest improvements on high-resolution benchmark: HR-Bench 4K shows only 2.5% gain over Qwen72B verdict baseline (75.6% vs 73.1%), limiting practical significance for this task

Incomplete ablations: no explicit ablation isolating consensus selection impact vs. simply using all k=5 models with varying m, no ablation comparing relative NLL to absolute NLL or other scoring schemes

Structured input preprocessing adds unexplained complexity: PP-StructureV3 required for information-intensive benchmarks, Table 10 shows marginal benefit yet still introduces additional pipeline component

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 4 diverse benchmarks with extensive ablation studies demonstrating consistent improvements
Clear problem motivation with concrete examples of information-intensive visual reasoning challenges
Interesting empirical finding: recovers 47-53% of minority-correct cases where majority voting and verdict alone fail, showing error decomposition
Well-written presentation with clear visualizations and good reproducibility (code release, detailed prompts, implementation details)
Practical training-free approach allowing flexible model selection across benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward combination of existing techniques (multiple models, CoT prompting, NLL consensus scoring, large model synthesis) without significant algorithmic innovation
Weak theoretical foundation: key claim that 'consensus indicates reliability' is asserted without empirical validation; no analysis of when/why method works or fails
Consensus scoring heuristic lacks justification: why should NLL-based agreement correlate with correctness? Different models may share training distribution biases and converge on incorrect answers

Incomplete computational cost analysis: requires 9 model passes per sample (5 candidates + 3 drafts + 1 verdict) but paper doesn't compare total inference cost vs. single large model with optimized prompting
Modest empirical improvements: 3-6% gains on main benchmarks (Table 1) are incremental; 10-11% gains over verdict largely reflect leveraging draft models rather than novel algorithm
Unfair experimental setup: PP-StructureV3 preprocessing provides auxiliary information (layout-aware structured representations) not available to baselines, potentially biasing comparisons

Limited failure mode analysis: paper shows when SV succeeds but not why; zero-correct recovery only 2.5-4.5% indicates method fundamentally relies on some correct signal; no systematic analysis of failure cases
Design choices lack justification: why NLL-based consensus over alternatives? Why m=3 experts (may be dataset-specific)? Why this prompting strategy? No prompt sensitivity analysis
Questionable generalization: all benchmarks are VQA on information-intensive images; unclear generalization to general VQA, other vision-language tasks, or out-of-distribution scenarios
Incomplete baseline comparisons: only one tool-driven method (DeepEyes); missing recent ensemble/synthesis methods; no structured reasoning baselines
Verdict model advantage: GPT-4o provides significant edge; Table 3 shows smaller verdicts (GLM-4.1V-9B) give only modest gains, raising questions about robustness
Loose connection to speculative decoding: analogy is superficial—speculative decoding optimizes speed while this optimizes accuracy; theoretical motivation for why adaptation should work is missing

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 diverse benchmarks with thorough ablation studies demonstrating consistent improvements (3.6-11.9% gains over strong baselines)
Impressive error correction capability, recovering 47-53% of minority-correct cases where verdict alone fails, with compelling qualitative examples (Figures 3, 10)
Well-motivated problem formulation identifying real challenges in information-intensive VQA and clear intuitive methodology with efficient consensus-based expert selection
Strong cost-efficiency with single verdict call per image (~$0.007 with GPT-4o) while achieving state-of-the-art results, outperforming proprietary models
Excellent reproducibility with comprehensive implementation details, prompt templates, ablations on model pool compositions, and commitment to code release
Training-free and generalizable approach that works across different model scales (2-4B to 7-9B) and extends to high-resolution images
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—core contribution is primarily an application of existing speculative decoding to multimodal reasoning rather than novel technical mechanisms
Consensus scoring mechanism lacks theoretical justification; no analysis of when/why NLL-based consensus correlates with answer correctness or fails in edge cases
Heavy dependence on strong verdict models (GPT-4o performs best; Qwen-72B noticeably weaker) undermines cost-efficiency claims and limits practical accessibility
Insufficient analysis of reasoning path generation quality; assumes draft experts produce structured reasoning paths but sensitivity to reasoning path quality not studied
Zero-correct recovery mechanism (2.5-4.5%) is under-explained; unclear how verdict extracts signal from entirely incorrect reasoning paths
External preprocessing dependency on PP-StructureV3 creates gap between 'training-free' claim and practical implementation; necessity and benefits not well characterized
Limited failure mode analysis—no discussion of when method fails, when consensus is wrong, or which question types remain challenging
Design choice justification lacking: k=5 and m=3 hyperparameters not motivated; cross-all selection strategy compared only to best-reference

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear illustration of challenges in information-intensive VQA (Figure 1)
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across four benchmarks with diverse baselines (proprietary, open-source, tool-driven)
Training-free practical framework with strong empirical results: 11.9% improvement over GPT-4o on InfographicVQA and effective error recovery (47-53% of minority-correct cases)
Extensive supplementary analysis including complementarity studies (Appendix I), failure mode analysis (Appendix J), and multiple ablations
Cost-efficient approach achieving better performance than o1 with 15-26% of its computational cost
Insightful analysis showing division of labor across draft experts and complementary reasoning strengths (Tables 23-25)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of ensemble methods and synthesis; connection to speculative decoding is inspirational but not fundamental—solves different problem (accuracy vs. speed)

Consensus expert selection mechanism lacks strong theoretical justification: why should NLL-based peer agreement correlate with correctness? Sensitive to calibration (Table 15 shows collapse without normalization)
Incomplete cost-efficiency analysis: reported costs exclude draft generation expenses; full pipeline cost should include k draft models + 1 verdict, making comparison to baselines less favorable

Generalization limitations: smaller improvements on non-intensive benchmarks (3.0-2.6% on TallyQA/MathVista vs. 6.7-11.9% on information-intensive tasks); method appears domain-specific; evaluation limited to English information-intensive VQA

Failure modes (Table 26) reveal fundamental VLM limitations (88% are fine-grained extraction and color matching errors) not addressed by SV's design, suggesting method is capped by underlying capabilities
Verdict synthesis vs. selection not deeply investigated: gains over LLaVA-Critic-7B are modest (0.5-6.6% with equal 7B backbone, Table 17); unclear if synthesis or model scale drives improvements
Limited exploration of alternatives: no investigation of learned aggregators, diversity-based selection, or alternative ensemble methods; simple 'cross-all' strategy is fairly basic
Calibration sensitivity: normalization critical for method stability but appears somewhat ad-hoc; raises questions about robustness across different model pools and architectures

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks (InfographicVQA, ChartMuseum, ChartQAPro, HR-Bench 4K) with strong baselines including GPT-4o
Thorough ablation studies and supplementary analysis (draft complementarity, failure modes, recovery patterns)
Practical cost-efficiency: achieves gains over GPT-4o at 15-26% of o1's inference cost
Clear presentation of core idea with effective visualizations (Figures 1-3)
Well-motivated problem addressing genuine challenges in information-intensive VQA
Useful practical framework that could benefit practitioners on dense visual reasoning tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward application of speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023) to multimodal reasoning without clear articulation of novel contributions beyond this adaptation

Critical evaluation fairness issue: verdict model receives PP-StructureV3 structured input that baselines do not, providing substantial (~4.7%) unfair advantage (Appendix H.2). Main comparisons should include all methods with/without this input

Misleading 'error correction' claims: recovery rates are calculated only among verdict-failure cases, minority-correct cases represent ~2-6% of total test set, and absolute improvement is modest. Gains primarily from stronger verdict model + additional reasoning paths, not novel error correction

Verdict stage effectiveness driven by model strength, not framework: gains drop significantly with weaker verdicts (Table 4, Table 8), suggesting improvements come from using GPT-4o rather than the SV design itself

Overclaimed contributions: 'training-free' is marketing speak (requires pre-trained models); 'synthesis' is really just better prompting of a stronger model; lacks principled justification for why consensus-based selection or verdict synthesis should work

Consensus selection mechanism insufficiently justified: NLL-based agreement is ad-hoc; limited ablations on alternatives; Table F.2 reveals critical dependence on normalization, indicating calibration issues undermining the premise
Draft complementarity analysis anecdotal: only 50 hand-annotated cases for manual categorization (Table 24); no systematic evidence that complementarity is the source of improvements

Limited generalization: strong gains on dense VQA (4-11% over GPT-4o) but modest improvements on MathVista (1.5%) and TallyQA (1.5%); unclear if framework applies broadly beyond information-intensive visual reasoning

LLaVA-Critic comparison concerning: even 72B model underperforms SV (Table 20), suggesting advantages may come from GPT-4o architecture rather than framework; open-source verdict comparison shows more modest gains (0.5-6.6%)
Failure mode analysis reveals fundamental limitations: 52.9% fine-grained extraction errors, 35.3% color matching errors are inherent VLM limitations that concatenating reasoning paths does not solve
Model pool selection and hyperparameters lack principled justification: why these 5 models? Why m=3? Only empirical tuning shown in Figure 5, not design principles
Key information hidden: importance of structured input preprocessing should be in main paper, not buried in Appendix H.2; total contribution from this auxiliary input obscured
No code provided despite reproducibility claims; prompt templates in appendix insufficient for full reproduction

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four benchmarks with consistent improvements (4-11% over draft experts, 6.6-12% over GPT-4o) and strong cost-efficiency (15-26% of o1's cost)
Well-motivated framework that creatively adapts speculative decoding to address real challenges in information-intensive visual reasoning (localization and multi-hop reasoning)
Excellent empirical analysis showing 47-53% recovery of minority-correct cases (Figure 4) and detailed complementarity analysis demonstrating genuine expert specialization (Tables 24-25)
Training-free approach with comprehensive reproducibility details including prompts, configurations, and promised code release
Practical impact: demonstrates cost-efficient multimodal reasoning without fine-tuning, relevant for real-world VLM deployment
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: consensus scoring via NLL is straightforward, verdict stage is standard chain-of-thought prompting; primary contribution is in combination rather than novel components

Consensus mechanism design lacks principled justification: NLL normalization choice appears post-hoc (F.2), cross-all selection strategy is greedy without theoretical grounding, hyperparameter m=3 somewhat arbitrary
Critical dependency on verdict model quality: smaller verdicts significantly degrade performance despite 60-200× more output tokens (Table 4), limiting applicability when strong models unavailable

Incomplete analysis of complementarity: manual analysis covers only 50 instances, no systematic method to select diverse experts beyond using consensus as proxy, low zero-correct recovery (2.5-4.5%) suggests mechanism primarily amplifies consensus rather than synthesizing diverse signals

Statistical rigor concerns: no confidence intervals or significance testing, some improvements modest (1.3% on ChartMuseum), only 1000 samples for o1 comparison, multiple benchmarks use different random samples
Generalization limitations: evaluated only on VQA tasks with single correct answers; consensus mechanism assumes unique correct answer, limiting applicability to open-ended generation tasks

Incomplete computational analysis: actual inference latency not reported, overhead of k=5 draft forward passes plus reasoning generation not quantified, API cost comparison to o1 favorable but potentially misleading for actual deployment timing
Prompt engineering sensitivity: benchmark-specific prompts required (Figure 10) but robustness not systematically studied; structured input preprocessing added despite marginal benefit (H.2)
